text: Education in Socrates' city begins with stories, since children hear them before they are trained in gymnastics (Republic II, 376e–377a). The founders must therefore supervise the makers of stories, and Socrates lays down two laws (typoi) governing what may be said about the gods. The first is that God is good, and is for that reason the cause of good things only (379b–c). Nothing good can do harm. Since the evils in human life far outnumber the goods, some other cause must be found for them. The second law is that God neither changes nor deceives (380d–381e). Whatever is in the best condition is least altered by anything acting on it from outside, and a perfect being would never willingly change for the worse. Three exclusions follow. Homer's two jars standing at the threshold of Zeus must go (379d). Any poet who says a god brought ruin on a household must go with them, and so must every tale of gods who change their shape. The lie that gods and human beings hate most is the lie in the soul, which Socrates ranks above any lie spoken aloud. It consists in being deceived about what is real in the most important part of oneself (382a–b). A god has no such lie within him, and no motive to plant one in anyone else.
